title: How To Love Unlikable Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: In one of his most personal essays, Linsin describes his first year of teaching and his relationship with a defiant fourth grader named Anthony, whose disruptive, sometimes cruel behavior initially provoked resentment rather than compassion. The turning point comes when Linsin learns Anthony was living in the backseat of a car with his mother and younger sister, an experience that leads him to confront his own selfishness and recommit to never taking student behavior personally again. From this experience he distills several lessons: that students sense when a teacher dislikes them, that resentment undermines a teacher's ability to help or manage a classroom, that understanding pain behind extreme behavior softens judgment, and that difficult students still need to be held accountable rather than excused. The essay closes on a note of redemption, describing how the rest of the school year with Anthony became a success built on laughter and genuine affection.
points: Students can sense when a teacher secretly dislikes them, and that perception undermines the relationship regardless of what is said aloud.
Resentment toward a difficult student sabotages a teacher's ability to help that student or manage the classroom effectively.
Recognizing that extreme behavior often stems from real pain or hardship can soften a teacher's judgment without excusing the behavior.
Difficult students still need consequences and accountability — indulgence is not the same as compassion.
Difficult students often crave being treated the same as everyone else, including receiving genuine, not excessive, praise.
quotes: If you don’t like them, they’ll know it. You can’t hide negative thoughts about students for long.
Dislike or resentment toward students will sabotage your ability to help them or effectively manage your classroom.
And then I found out he lived in the backseat of a car. He shared it with his five-year-old sister, and his mom slept in the front seat. He never knew his father.

I sat in my car in the school parking lot and cried. I was ashamed of my behavior and my selfishness, and I vowed to focus on helping students like Anthony and never taking their behavior personally again.
You’re not doing difficult students any favors by overlooking poor behavior and neglecting to hold them accountable.
Having Anthony in my class my first year of teaching was the best thing that could have happened to me, and I’m grateful for the lessons I learned from him.
